# Into Kentucky

We were driving into Kentucky, deep in the humid embrace of the South, when Kay finally gave voice to what had been weighing on her. She turned to me and said, plainly, that she didn't think we should raise mixed-race children in a place like this. The words hung in the thick air between us, heavy with everything they implied about the world we were passing through.

As if summoned by her fears, a truck roared up and cut in front of us. A Confederate flag hung from it, snapping in the wind. In the bed of the truck sat a thin, shirtless blond boy, his pale skin exposed to the sun. He kept his eyes averted, refusing to meet our gaze, as though he too understood something about the moment we shared with him on that road.

Something ignited in me. A fury I hadn't expected surged through my chest, and with it came violent fantasies I couldn't suppress. I wanted to deface that flag, to tear it down and destroy what it stood for. My imagination went further still—I pictured the truck careening off the road, tumbling into a ravine, disappearing from our lives entirely. The intensity of my own anger surprised me, but I couldn't will it away.

Eventually, I pressed the accelerator and moved to pass them. And then something unexpected happened. As we drew alongside, the boy in the back looked up and smiled at us. He raised his hand and waved—a genuine, uncomplicated gesture. The driver, meanwhile, stared fixedly ahead, his eyes locked on the road, never once acknowledging our presence.

Beside me, Kay was struggling with her own emotions. I watched her face flush red, watched her hands curl into tight fists in her lap. Her distress was visible, undeniable, written plainly across her body as we left the truck behind us and continued on into Kentucky.
outputs.L4:
The highway unspooled ahead of us like a gray ribbon, cutting through the thickening green of the South. Kay had been quiet for the last hour, her gaze fixed on the passing fields and the occasional weathered barn, but I could feel something building in her, the way you sense a storm before the first drop of rain.

"Do you ever think about what it'll be like for them?" she finally asked, not turning from the window.

"For who?"

"Our kids. If we have them." She pressed her palm flat against the glass. "Growing up looking the way they'll look. In a place that looks like this."

I didn't have an answer ready, so I said nothing. The truth was I thought about it all the time—the questions people would ask, the assumptions they'd make, the small cruelties and the large ones. But saying it aloud felt like handing her a weight I wasn't sure she could carry, not here, not on this stretch of road where the world felt both endless and closing in.

That was when we saw the truck.

It sat ahead of us in the right lane, a hulking thing riding high on oversized tires, its paint faded to the color of rust and old blood. And there, mounted above the tailgate and snapping in the wind, was the Confederate flag—that unmistakable X of stars against red, the symbol that meant so many different things to so many different people, none of them comforting to a woman like Kay.

She went rigid beside me. I watched her jaw tighten, watched her hands curl slowly into fists in her lap.

"Just pass it," she said quietly. "Please."

I checked my mirror and eased into the left lane, accelerating to draw even with the truck. As we came alongside, I saw them: a man behind the wheel, sunburned and stone-faced, his eyes fixed on the road ahead as though we didn't exist at all. And in the bed of the truck, sitting cross-legged among coils of rope and a red plastic cooler, was a boy. He couldn't have been more than seven or eight, all gap-toothed grin and windblown hair.

The boy caught sight of us and lit up. He lifted his small hand and waved—waved with the pure, uncomplicated joy of a child who had not yet learned what that flag above his head was supposed to mean, who saw only strangers on a summer afternoon and wanted, simply, to say hello.

I felt my chest ache with the impossible contradiction of it. The boy waving. The flag whipping. The father staring straight ahead, refusing to acknowledge us, as if his silence were its own kind of message.

Beside me, Kay's fists were clenched so tightly that her knuckles had gone pale. She didn't wave back. She couldn't. She stared at the boy and the flag and the unmoving profile of the man, and I saw everything she was feeling flicker across her face—the anger, yes, but beneath it something rawer and more tender, a grief for the world we were driving deeper into, and for the children we might one day bring into it.

I pressed the accelerator harder. The truck fell away behind us, the boy's small figure shrinking in the mirror until the road curved and swallowed him whole.

For a long moment neither of us spoke. Then Kay unclenched her hands, one finger at a time, and let out a breath she seemed to have been holding for miles.

"He didn't know," she said. "The boy. He didn't know."

"No," I agreed. "He didn't."

And somehow that was the hardest part of all.

# The Enduring Charm of the South: Kay's Journey Through Kentucky

The American South holds a special place in the hearts of many, and few states capture its essence quite like Kentucky. Known for its rolling bluegrass hills, rich history, and warm hospitality, Kentucky embodies the spirit of Southern living in ways both timeless and unique.

## Kay's Discovery

Kay had always dreamed of exploring the South, and Kentucky became her perfect starting point. As a first-time visitor, she was immediately struck by the state's natural beauty—the emerald pastures dotted with grazing horses, the winding country roads, and the majestic thoroughbred farms that stretched as far as the eye could see.

## A State of Contrasts

What Kay appreciated most about Kentucky was its wonderful blend of traditions and progress. The South, often stereotyped in popular culture, revealed itself to be far more nuanced through her travels. Kentucky offered:

- **Horse Country**: The famous Kentucky Derby and countless horse farms
- **Bourbon Heritage**: The historic distilleries along the Bourbon Trail
- **Musical Roots**: Bluegrass music that echoes through the mountains
- **Culinary Delights**: From hot browns to fried chicken and cornbread

## Southern Hospitality

Perhaps the most memorable aspect of Kay's journey was the genuine kindness she encountered. The people of Kentucky welcomed her with open arms, sharing stories over sweet tea and pointing her toward hidden gems that no guidebook could reveal. This warmth is what defines the Southern experience—a sense of community and belonging that transcends geography.

## Conclusion

For Kay, Kentucky became more than just a destination in the South; it became a place that captured her imagination and left an indelible impression on her heart. Whether you're drawn by the horses, the history, or simply the promise of Southern charm, Kentucky stands ready to welcome you, just as it welcomed Kay.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short piece of literary flash fiction about a mixed-race couple driving through the American South and encountering a truck with a Confederate flag.
counterfactuals.output:
# Two-Lane Blacktop

The truck appeared in the rearview first, a red smear that resolved into chrome and rust as it closed the distance. Deja saw the flag before David did—that familiar cross of stars snapping against the Georgia heat, mounted in the bed like a threat or a prayer.

"Speed up," she said, then hated herself for saying it.

David's hands stayed easy on the wheel. He'd grown up here, in a town they'd passed an hour ago, and he read these roads like liturgy. "He just wants to pass."

The truck rode their bumper for a mile of pine and kudzu. Deja kept her eyes forward, cataloging the exits, the gas stations, the distance to anywhere. Beside her, David was doing something she'd watched him do at his mother's dinner table, at the DMV, in the delivery room when their daughter came sideways into the world: he was making himself into a still, calm thing, a lake nobody could see the bottom of.

The flag filled the mirror.

She thought about their girl, asleep at David's sister's house, her hair a negotiation between them, her skin a color that didn't exist on any government form. She thought about how love had felt, at twenty-two, like enough. Like a country you could build with two people and defend forever.

Then the truck swung wide into the passing lane.

It idled alongside for one held breath. Deja looked—she couldn't help it—and saw the driver. An old man. Sunspotted, gray-stubbled, his face a roadmap of some private erosion. He didn't glance over. Didn't sneer or spit or do any of the things her body had already braced against. He was just a tired man in a truck, going somewhere, hauling his history behind him like a load he'd forgotten how to unhook.

He pulled ahead and shrank into the shimmer.

David exhaled. Deja realized she'd been gripping the door handle, her knuckles pale as bone.

"See?" David said, but his voice cracked on the word, and she understood then that his stillness had cost him too—that he'd been holding the same breath, running the same calculus, that the calm was a thing he'd been forced to build rather than something he owned.

She put her hand on his thigh. Outside, the South unspooled: churches and cotton, dollar stores and dogwoods, all of it beautiful and none of it safe.

"Almost there," she said.

Neither of them believed it, and both of them held on.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a first-person prose vignette exploring race, tension, and a fleeting encounter on a road trip into Kentucky. Use vivid sensory imagery and a rhythm of repeated "I want" statements.
counterfactuals.output:
The Kentucky Line

I want to tell you about the heat first, how it came up off the asphalt in visible waves, how it bent the horizon into something liquid and untrustworthy. I want you to feel the vinyl seat sticking to the backs of my thighs, the way my skin peeled away from it with a sound like something tearing.

We crossed into Kentucky around noon. The radio had gone to static an hour back, and my mother let it hiss because the silence felt worse. I watched the tobacco fields unspool, green and enormous, the leaves broad as dinner plates, and I thought about hands. I thought about whose hands had worked this ground, generations of them, and I want to say I understood something then, but I was thirteen and mostly I understood thirst.

The gas station sat at a crossroads with no other buildings in sight. A Confederate flag hung in the window, faded to the color of old blood, and my mother's grip tightened on the wheel. I saw her jaw work. I saw her decide.

I want to tell you we drove past. We didn't. The tank was near empty and the next town was a question mark on a folded map.

Inside, the air conditioning was a mercy and a warning both. A man stood behind the counter, older, his face weathered into deep grooves, his eyes the pale blue of a boiled sky. I want to say he glared. I want to say he made it easy, made himself a villain I could carry home like a souvenir of my own righteousness.

But he looked at my mother, and something in his face moved. Not warmth. Not that. Something more complicated, a flicker, a reckoning happening behind his eyes that I would spend years trying to name.

"Hot one," he said.

"Yes," my mother said. Just that.

I want to tell you what passed between them in that small hot room, but I only have the pieces. The way he counted her change slow and careful, coins pressed into her palm without the flinch I'd learned to expect, without the dropping of money onto the counter to avoid the touch of her skin. The way he said "y'all drive safe now," and meant the "safe" differently than the words usually meant it, meant it like a man who knew what roads could do to people who looked like us.

I want to make him simple. I cannot make him simple.

Back in the car, my mother sat a moment with her hands in her lap. The flag still hung in that window. Both things were true at once, the flag and the coins in her palm, and I understood that I would have to hold two truths at the same time for the rest of my life, that this was the whole grief and gift of it.

I want to tell you it changed him. It didn't. He went home to whatever house held that flag's twin.

I want to tell you it changed me. That I'm not sure of either. But I remember the weight of those coins. I remember the fields going by after, green and patient and full of the dead. I remember wanting, more than water, more than shade, to live in a country that did not require me to be surprised by decency.

I want that still.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical, poetic flash fiction scene (under 250 words) narrated by someone whose partner says they shouldn't raise mixed babies in the South.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Soil Remembers**

You say it over collard greens gone cold between us, your fork a small surrender against the plate. *We can't raise them here.*

Outside, the magnolias are lying again, all that white perfume over roots that drink from graves. You grew up learning which sidewalks belonged to you. I grew up not learning, which was its own kind of lesson.

I want to tell you about my grandmother's hands, brown as riverbed, planting okra in Alabama clay because leaving felt like letting them win. I want to tell you the South is not one thing. It is my mother's hymns and the cousin who won't come to our wedding. It is honeysuckle and it is rope. It holds both. It always has.

You reach across the table and I let you. Your fingers, pale as the underside of leaves, thread through mine, and we make that old impossible color, the one they built fences against.

*Somewhere else,* you say, *they could just be children.*

But children aren't grown in safety. They're grown in truth, and I want ours rooted deep enough to survive the weather. I want them to know this land that made me, the way you love a difficult mother.

Fireflies rise in the yard like the dead deciding to shine anyway.

I press your knuckles to my mouth.

*Then let's teach them,* I whisper, *to bloom where they told us we couldn't.*

The night leans close, listening, and does not answer.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a piece of creative nonfiction or fiction capturing the anger and helplessness of driving past a Confederate flag while thinking about interracial love and children.
counterfactuals.output:
**Sixty-Two Miles of County Road**

The flag comes up on the right, just past the feed store, hung from a pole bolted to the porch of a house that leans like it's tired of standing. It's the size of a bedsheet. Somebody wanted it seen.

I don't slow down. I don't speed up. I do the thing I've trained myself to do, which is keep my hands at ten and two and my eyes forward and my face arranged into nothing. But my body does what my body does. The tightening under the ribs. The heat climbing my neck like it has somewhere to be.

David is asleep in the passenger seat, his head tipped against the window, and I am grateful he doesn't see me see it. Twelve years married and he still can't fully understand this, the way a piece of cloth can reach into a car doing fifty-five and put its hand around your throat. He's tried. God knows he's tried. But you can't learn a thing in your nose that another person learned in their blood.

I think about our daughter. She's not born yet, not even conceived, just a conversation we keep having in the dark. What she'll look like. Whose eyes. I think about how I already love her, this argument-in-progress, this maybe. And I think about that flag flapping over a road she might one day drive down, and I feel something crack open in me that is not sadness, exactly. Sadness is soft. This has edges.

Here is what the anger is: it is the knowledge that somebody hung that flag *at* people. Not for heritage, not for a great-great-grandfather who died cold and stupid in a field for the right to own human beings. At *me.* At the two of us in this car, my brown hand and his white one that will make a child neither of us can fully protect. The flag is a sentence with no verb, and the verb is understood. *You. Should not.*

And here is what the helplessness is: I will drive past it. That's the whole thing. I will pass it at fifty-five and it will still be there when I'm gone, and it will be there tomorrow, and it does not care one inch that my heart is a fist right now. My rage is a private weather. It changes nothing on that porch. The flag doesn't know I exist and that is somehow the worst part—that I can be reduced to nothing by something that isn't even *aimed,* the way a stone doesn't aim to break your teeth.

I imagine stopping. I do this every time. I imagine pulling into the gravel and walking up those tired steps and asking whoever's inside, *Do you know what this is? Do you know what it says to a woman like me?* And I imagine the face at the door, and I know the face already, I've seen the face my whole life, and the face would say *It's just history* or the face would say *You people always* or the face would say nothing and just look, the way you look at a dog that's gotten into the yard.

So I don't stop. I keep my hands at ten and two.

David stirs. "Where are we?" he asks, thick with sleep.

"About an hour out," I say, and my voice comes out level, which is its own small violence, the effort of it.

He takes my hand off the wheel, kisses my knuckles, puts it back. He didn't see. He gets to not have seen. I love him and I could scream, both at once, the loving and the screaming pouring through the same narrow place.

The flag is behind us now. In the mirror it's just a red smudge, then gone behind the trees.

I think about our daughter one more time before I let her go for the day. I think: *I will teach you to keep your hands at ten and two. And I will hate that I have to. And I will teach you anyway.* Because the flag will still be there when she learns to drive, or one like it, on some other porch, and I cannot burn them all down no matter how much of me wants to, and the wanting is not a plan, the wanting is just the fire I carry so I don't go numb.

Sixty-two miles of county road. I count them. It's the only thing I can do with my hands that helps.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an intense, image-driven short narrative about two women driving through the South, seeing a blond boy in the back of a pickup truck with a Confederate flag, and the complicated emotions it stirs.
counterfactuals.output:
# Heat Lightning

The blond boy couldn't have been more than nine.

Dessa saw him first, though she didn't say anything, just let her foot ease off the gas so the rental car dropped back into the truck's slipstream. Georgia in August. The AC wheezed against a losing war, and the asphalt ahead rippled like something underwater.

The pickup's tailgate hung down. The boy sat with his sneakers dangling, kicking at the air, and behind him the flag snapped and cracked in the wind—that flag, red and blue and crossed with stars, mounted on a pole bolted to the truck bed like it had grown there.

"Don't," Marguerite said.

"I'm not doing anything."

"You're doing something with your face."

Dessa laughed, but it came out wrong, more air than sound. Twenty years they'd known each other. Marguerite could read her like weather.

The boy was eating a popsicle. Red, so the color ran down his wrist and he licked at it, unbothered, squinting into the sun. He had that particular gold hair that only children have, the kind that darkens by twelve and is gone forever. His face was open as a window.

*He doesn't know,* Dessa thought, and then hated the thought, because that was the lie people told. *He's just a kid. He doesn't know what it means.*

But somebody had bolted that pole to that truck. Somebody had raised him under it.

"My grandmother," Marguerite started, then stopped.

Dessa waited. The road unspooled. A billboard for boiled peanuts. A church with a marquee: HE IS RISEN, ARE YOU?

"My grandmother wouldn't drive this stretch," Marguerite finished. "Not this exact road. She'd go forty miles around. I used to think she was being dramatic."

The boy waved.

He waved at them, actually waved, the popsicle hand, sticky and red, swinging back and forth with a grin that had a gap in it where a tooth had come out. Just a boy in the back of a truck, delighted by the ladies in the car behind, wanting to be seen.

Dessa's hand lifted off the wheel before she could stop it.

She didn't wave back. She just—raised it. Held it there, halfway. Caught between something. The heat came through the windshield and pressed against her face and she thought about her own hands, her own grandmother's hands, the stories folded up inside her like letters in a drawer she never opened because opening them cost too much.

The boy waved harder, delighted by even this.

"God," Marguerite said softly. "Look at him. He's just—" She didn't finish.

"I know."

"He's beautiful."

"I know."

And that was the whole terrible thing, wasn't it. That he *was.* That you could hold both in your two hands at once, the child and the cloth above him, the innocence and the inheritance, and neither one canceled the other out. The flag didn't make him less of a child. The child didn't make the flag less of what it was. They rode down the highway together, boy and banner, and Dessa couldn't unsee either one.

She let her hand fall back to the wheel.

The truck's blinker came on—orange, blinking, patient—and it slowed for a turn onto some red dirt road that ran off between the pines toward wherever he lived, whatever house, whatever people. The boy braced himself against the wheel well as the truck banked. He was still watching them. Still waving. Growing smaller.

Dessa drove straight on.

In the mirror she watched the flag shrink and flicker through the trees, red then gone, red then gone, like something signaling. Like heat lightning on a night with no rain in it—all that flash and no storm, no relief, just the sky showing you it could burn.

"You okay?" Marguerite asked.

Dessa thought about it. Gave her friend the truth, which was the only thing twenty years had earned between them.

"No," she said. "But keep the map out. I don't want to miss the turn."

They drove north into the long gold afternoon, and neither of them waved, and neither of them forgot the small hand in the mirror, reaching for them across all that distance, wanting only to be waved back at.

Some part of Dessa was still lifting her hand.

Some part of her never would.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
